text: Amazon S3 is where almost everything in AWS ends up storing its files. This lesson covers the three ideas that make S3 click: the bucket, the object, and the storage classes that decide what you pay for how fast you can get data back.

An S3 bucket is the top-level container, and its name has to be unique across every AWS account on the planet, not just your own — because bucket names form part of a real, predictable URL. aws s3api create-bucket with --bucket and --region creates one, and that Region is where the data physically stays unless you set up replication later.

Inside a bucket, an object is the actual file plus its metadata, and every object is identified by a key — a string like invoices/2026/october-summary.pdf. S3 has no real folder hierarchy underneath a bucket, the same flat-namespace design the prior Azure course covered for blob containers; the slashes are just characters the console renders as folders. Underneath, every object sits directly in the bucket, addressed by its full key.

Uploading an object lets you pick its storage class right on the command: aws s3 cp with --storage-class GLACIER sends that file straight to the cheapest, coldest tier instead of the default. That one flag is the entire decision point for cost versus retrieval speed.

S3 Standard is the default — highest storage cost, but millisecond retrieval with no retrieval fee, for data you touch regularly. Standard-IA costs less to store and still reads in milliseconds, but charges a per-GB fee when you actually retrieve it. Glacier is the cheapest by far, but retrieval takes minutes to hours depending on the tier you choose — you're trading speed away entirely for the lowest possible cost.

Buckets, objects, keys, and three storage classes — that's the foundation every other S3 feature builds on, and it's the same vocabulary you'll use whether you're clicking through the console or scripting it with the CLI. Next up: versioning, lifecycle rules, and the access control layers that keep a bucket from becoming an accidental public leak.
